newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Peacekeepers with tanks extend patrols in Liberia.
newsitem.headline: Peacekeepers with tanks extend patrols in Liberia.

text.p: West African troops backed by tanks extended patrols in western Liberia on Thursday after rebels blocking highways melted into the bush as peacekeepers moved close to them, commanders said.
"We left some units behind after yesterday's operation and they are patrolling further inland," said the commander of the Nigerian-led ECOMOG peacekeeping force, General Victor Malu.
"We'll continue patrols and keep the roads open and safe for relief workers to resume food distribution," Malu told Reuters.
Truckloads of chanting ECOMOG troops rolled out into western Liberia on Wednesday to clear out ULIMO-J guerrillas loyal to warlord General Roosevelt Johnson.
A military spokesman said troops encountered no rebels as they swept into the hinterland and fanned out towards Cape Mount County and the town of Tubmanburg.
Hundreds of frightened and starving villagers, including many who had sheltered in the bush to escape rampaging rebels, emerged to welcome the troops, reporters in the convoy said.
ECOMOG had vowed to use force to evict the rebels if they did not dismantle roadblocks by Wednesday.
Tubmanburg, a stronghold of Johnson's Krahn tribe, is at the heart of the most volatile region in Liberia, which has been devastated by civil war since December 1989.
Ethnic militia rivalry is intense around Tubmanburg, whose outlying area once produced the bulk of Liberia's wealth in diamonds and timber.
Battles between ECOMOG and ULIMO-J in the region last December and January were followed by militia warfare in Monrovia in April and May that derailed a 1995 peace accord.
Johnson was at the centre of the Monrovia fighting, which followed his sacking from the cabinet and an attempt by the interim government to arrest him on murder charges.
He has since been reinstated in the government under measures to put the peace process back on track, but has not commented on the latest activities of his followers.
An ULIMO-J spokesman pleaded on Wednesday for time for ULIMO-J guerrillas to withdraw from highways.
A West African summit in Nigeria last August pressured Liberia's squabbling warlords to sign a new accord providing for disarament of 60,000 guerrillas and elections by May next year.
Despite symbolic gestures and promises of disarmament, the process has yet to take off in earnest as ECOMOG says it is waiting for troops reinforcements from regional states.
More than 150,000 people have died in the conflict in Liberia, which was founded by freed American slaves in 1847 as Africa's first independent republic.
